title: Auditory Disabilities – Hearing the Web 🔊
description: Deafness, hard of hearing, and the importance of captions, transcripts, and visual alerts.

slides.title: Deaf & Hard of Hearing 🦻
slides.content:
Auditory disabilities range from mild hearing loss to total deafness.

* Users may communicate via sign language, lip‑reading, or text.
* They rely on **visual alternatives** for audio content.
* Not all deaf users know sign language; captions are essential.

Web accessibility must ensure audio content is also available visually.

quizData.question: What is the most basic requirement for deaf users when a video has spoken content?
quizData.explanation: Captions provide a synchronised text alternative of the audio. Transcripts are also useful but captions are primary for video.

slides.title: Captions vs. Transcripts vs. Audio Description 🎬
slides.content:
* **Captions**: text synchronised with the video, including speaker identification and important sounds.
* **Transcripts**: full text version of all audio, separate from the video.
* **Audio description**: a narration of visual elements (for blind users) – not for deaf users, but part of inclusive media.

Always offer captions; transcripts are a plus.

quizData.question: A transcript alone is sufficient for a video with dialogue.
quizData.explanation: While a transcript is helpful, captions are required because they appear synchronised with the media, allowing deaf users to follow in real time.

slides.title: Audio Alerts & Notifications 🔔
slides.content:
If your app uses sounds to notify users (e.g., new message ping), ensure:

* A visual flash or badge accompanies the sound.
* Users can enable vibration or other haptic feedback on mobile.
* Avoid relying solely on audio to convey critical errors.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Caption Quality Matters

Auto‑generated captions are not enough. They often lack punctuation, speaker labels, and accuracy. Always review and edit them.
